title: Output Triage Clinic (Lab)
summary: Groups rotate through four output stations, diagnose each as correct, incorrect or unclear, choose a verification action, and rank them all on a trust ladder they must defend.
objectives: Apply a triage routine to a set of curated outputs and record correct/incorrect/unclear with reasons.
Rank outputs from most to least trustworthy and defend the order.
Choose a verification action for each untrustworthy output.

sections.heading: Output Triage Clinic (Lab)
body: Welcome to the triage clinic. Each output is a patient waiting for a diagnosis - correct, incorrect, or unclear - and a treatment: the action you would take to verify it. By the end you will have ranked them all on a trust ladder.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run the triage routine across a full set of outputs.
I can rank outputs by trustworthiness and defend my order.
I can choose a verification action for outputs I cannot trust.

terms.definition: Quickly sorting items by how they need to be handled.
The concrete step you take to check whether an output is true.
An ordering of outputs from most to least trustworthy.
Asking what could go wrong if an output were used as-is.

sections.heading: Match the check to the output
body: A fact needs a trusted source. A summary needs comparing back to the original text. A vague instruction needs a clearer prompt before you can even judge it.
Choosing the right check is what turns a guess into a verified judgement.

sections.heading: Rank and defend
body: After triaging, place your outputs on the [[trust ladder]] from most to least trustworthy.
Be ready to defend your order using signals, not preferences: what evidence puts one output above another?

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Rotate through four stations. Triage each output, choose a verification action, then rank them all on the trust ladder and prepare to defend your order.
items: Read the task and output at each station.
Assign a verdict and write a checkable reason.
Choose a verification action that fits the output type.
Rank all outputs on the trust ladder.
Agree your group's defence and one risk of the least trustworthy output.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which verification action was hardest to choose, and why?
Did any output move up or down the ladder after you discussed it?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write one verification action you will reuse in a future task.
Describe how you would explain your ranking to another group.

worksheet.title: Week 4 - Lab - Worksheet | Output Triage Clinic (Lab)

questions.prompt: At each clinic station, match the output to the verification action that fits it.

left.text: An output that states the Burj Khalifa is 828 m tall.
An output that summarises the article your group read at the station.
An output that says "follow the steps in the usual order" without listing any steps.
An output that says 4 tickets at 25 AED each cost 90 AED in total.

right.text: Look the height up in a trusted reference or official website.
Put it side by side with the original article and see whether it matches.
Write a clearer prompt asking for the steps to be listed one by one.
Work the calculation out yourself and compare the totals.

feedback.correct: Well matched - a claimed fact needs a trusted source, a summary needs the original text, a vague output needs a clearer prompt, and a calculation you can redo yourself.
feedback.incorrect: Match the check to the kind of output: facts go to a trusted source, summaries go back to the original text, vague outputs need re-prompting before they can be judged, and sums can simply be redone.

questions.prompt: Your group put Output A above Output B on the trust ladder. Which defence of that order uses a trust signal rather than a preference?

options.text: A gives a source we looked up and it matched; B states a number with no source anyone can check.
A is shorter and easier to read than B.
A sounds more sure of itself than B does.
Most of our group liked A better than B.

feedback.correct: That is a signal-based defence: it points to evidence - a source that was checked - that another group could check too.
feedback.incorrect: Length, confidence and what your group likes are preferences; a defence has to point to evidence, such as a source that was checked or a match to the task.

questions.prompt: Put the five steps of the clinic routine in the order your group should work through them.

items.text: Read the task and the output at the station.
Assign a verdict and write a checkable reason.
Choose a verification action that fits that type of output.
Rank all the outputs on the trust ladder.
Agree your group's defence of the order and one risk of the least trustworthy output.

feedback.correct: Yes - you can only rank outputs against each other once every one of them has its own verdict, reason and check.
feedback.incorrect: Each output is triaged and given a check first; the ladder compares outputs, so it can only be built after every station has a verdict and reason, and the defence comes last.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the outputs that belong near the BOTTOM of the trust ladder, as the least trustworthy.

options.text: An output that gives a statistic but names no source, so nobody in the group can check it.
An output whose date clashes with the date printed on the station card.
An output that answers a different question from the one the task asked.
An output that matched the original article line by line when the group compared them.
An output that sets its answer out in a neatly labelled table.

feedback.correct: Good - no source, a clash with the station card, and answering the wrong task are all trust signals pushing an output down the ladder.
feedback.incorrect: Low trust comes from signals: nothing to check against, a clash with a source, or not answering the task. A neat table is only presentation, and an output that matched the original belongs near the top.

questions.prompt:
Complete the clinic's rule for choosing a check. Write one word in each gap.
A claimed fact needs a trusted ______, but a summary needs comparing back to the ______ text.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the check has to match the output: facts are checked against a trusted source, summaries against the text they came from.
feedback.incorrect: A fact is checked against a trusted source, but a summary can only be checked against the original text it was made from - a website cannot tell you whether the summary matches your article.

formative.targets: Directly checks 'identifies when outputs are incorrect or unclear'
formative.check: Completed clinic record sheet plus a defended trust-ladder ranking
formative.successCriteria: Triages the full set with valid reasons, chooses a verification action each, and defends a sensible ranking.
formative.evidence: Clinic record sheet and trust ladder photo.
